title: Hearing Hundreds of Neurons at Once
endLine: Electrode arrays hear populations together; never confuse sites, units, and animals.

scenes.tts: How do you listen to hundreds of neurons firing at once? One electrode in one cell catches only a single voice. Yet waves, oscillations, and odour patterns belong to whole populations acting together.
scenes.caption: How do you listen to hundreds of neurons firing at once? One electrode in one cell catches only a single voice. Yet waves, oscillations, and odour patterns belong to whole populations acting together.
scenes.visual: Dark neural tissue field filling most of the frame height on the left, paired with a live trace panel on the right (all schematic). One bright neuron sits under a single electrode tip with one spike trace while dozens of surrounding neurons stay dim; as the final sentence speaks, glowing waves, rhythmic pulses, and scattered odour patterns sweep across the whole crowd.
scenes.narration: How do you listen to hundreds of neurons firing at once? One electrode in one cell catches only a single voice. Yet waves, oscillations, and odour patterns belong to whole populations acting together.

scenes.visual: The carried neural field continues pulsing gently in the background as the title 'Hearing Hundreds of Neurons at Once' appears in large, full-opacity text and fades out.

scenes.tts: Instead of one electrode in one cell, tissue rests on an array or holds a probe. The original Neuropixels probe from twenty seventeen carries nine hundred sixty recording sites. All sit along one shank about ten millimetres long. Push it into a mouse brain, and you hear spikes from hundreds of neurons at once.
scenes.caption: Instead of one electrode in one cell, tissue rests on an array or holds a probe. The original Neuropixels probe from 2017 carries 960 recording sites. All sit along one shank about 10 mm long. Push it into a mouse brain, and you hear spikes from hundreds of neurons at once.
scenes.visual: In the carried tissue world, the single electrode transforms first into a flat grid of electrodes under a thin tissue sheet, then morphs into a slim vertical shank labelled 'Neuropixels (2017)' with 960 tiny site marks along a shank labelled 'about 10 mm' (schematic). As the shank slides smoothly into a mouse brain cross-section, rows of live spike traces light up together on the right panel (schematic).
scenes.narration: Instead of one electrode in one cell, tissue rests on an array or holds a probe. The original Neuropixels probe from 2017 carries 960 recording sites. All sit along one shank about 10 mm long. Push it into a mouse brain, and you hear spikes from hundreds of neurons at once.

scenes.tts: Hearing many neurons at once reveals a population pattern, a list of each cell's response. When a mouse smells odour A, one neuron fires, one stays quiet, and another fires a little. Do the same for odour B, and compare both lists. Two odours are represented similarly when many of the same neurons respond to both.
scenes.caption: Hearing many neurons at once reveals a population pattern, a list of each cell's response. When a mouse smells odour A, one neuron fires, one stays quiet, and another fires a little. Do the same for odour B, and compare both lists. Two odours are represented similarly when many of the same neurons respond to both.
scenes.visual: The carried neural field remains on the left; a drifting cloud labelled 'Odour A' sweeps across it as neurons brighten to different levels, filling a response list on the right (bright bar for fired, empty for quiet, small bar for fired a little; schematic). A second cloud labelled 'Odour B' sweeps across the same neurons to build a second list beside A, and matching active rows glow together to show overlap (schematic).
scenes.narration: Hearing many neurons at once reveals a population pattern, a list of each cell's response. When a mouse smells odour A, one neuron fires, one stays quiet, and another fires a little. Do the same for odour B, and compare both lists. Two odours are represented similarly when many of the same neurons respond to both.

scenes.tts: To build that list, sites feed channels, then sorted units. Spike sorting groups spikes by shape, each unit meant to be one neuron. Yet nine hundred sixty sites do not equal nine hundred sixty neurons. One neuron can reach several sites; one site can hear several. Quality scores catch only some errors; a unit can still merge or split neurons.
scenes.caption: To build that list, sites feed channels, then sorted units. Spike sorting groups spikes by shape, each unit meant to be one neuron. Yet 960 sites do not equal 960 neurons. One neuron can reach several sites; one site can hear several. Quality scores catch only some errors; a unit can still merge or split neurons.
scenes.visual: Zoom back onto the Neuropixels shank in the carried tissue field while a bottom chain lights up step by step: 'sites -> channels -> units -> neurons' (schematic). On the right trace panel, one neuron's spike appears on several neighbouring sites and one site picks up two neurons' spikes; raw spikes then sort by shape into colour-coded 'sorted units', then two nearby neurons visibly merge into one unit and one neuron splits into two units under a 'quality scores: partial check' tag (schematic).
scenes.narration: To build that list, sites feed channels, then sorted units. Spike sorting groups spikes by shape, each unit meant to be one neuron. Yet 960 sites do not equal 960 neurons. One neuron can reach several sites; one site can hear several. Quality scores catch only some errors; a unit can still merge or split neurons.

scenes.tts: Now check the next link in the chain, from units to animals. Suppose a study records three hundred sorted units from three mice. How many samples does it actually have?
scenes.caption: Now check the next link in the chain, from units to animals. Suppose a study records 300 sorted units from three mice. How many samples does it actually have?
scenes.visual: The carried field zooms out into three mouse outlines in a row, each holding a probe surrounded by glowing sorted-unit dots totalling 300 units across the three mice (schematic). The bottom chain extends to 'units -> animals', and a clear question banner settles at top: '300 units from three mice — how many samples?'
scenes.narration: Now check the next link in the chain, from units to animals. Suppose a study records 300 sorted units from three mice. How many samples does it actually have?

scenes.visual: Hold the three mouse outlines, their 300 glowing unit dots (schematic), and the question banner steady on screen; the dots pulse slowly while a subtle progress ring fills across the silent pause.

scenes.tts: Three, not three hundred. More units sharpen each animal's estimate, but they all still come from the same mouse. Only more animals add samples, so trustworthy analysis works at the animal level. Arrays hear populations together, but sites are not neurons, and sorted units are not animals.
scenes.caption: Three, not 300. More units sharpen each animal's estimate, but they all still come from the same mouse. Only more animals add samples, so trustworthy analysis works at the animal level. Arrays hear populations together, but sites are not neurons, and sorted units are not animals.
scenes.visual: Inside each of the three mouse outlines, the unit dots converge smoothly into one crisp animal-level bar per mouse, leaving exactly three bars labelled 'animal-level analysis' (schematic). As the guiding rule is spoken, the full carried chain 'sites -> channels -> units -> neurons -> animals' highlights each separate step.

scenes.tts: In nineteen ninety-one, Meister, Wong, Baylor, and Shatz laid isolated retinas on an array. They recorded up to one hundred ganglion cells at once from newborn ferrets and fetal cats. Nearby cells fired in nearly synchronous bursts, waves several hundred micrometres wide. In twenty twelve, Ackman, Burbridge, and Crair imaged live neonatal mice, showing waves are no dish artefact.
scenes.caption: In 1991, Meister, Wong, Baylor, and Shatz laid isolated retinas on an array. They recorded up to 100 ganglion cells at once from newborn ferrets and fetal cats. Nearby cells fired in nearly synchronous bursts, waves several hundred micrometres wide. In 2012, Ackman, Burbridge, and Crair imaged live neonatal mice, showing waves are no dish artefact.
scenes.visual: The carried flat electrode array reappears beneath an isolated retina sheet holding up to 100 ganglion cell dots (labelled '1991, isolated retina', schematic). A bright wave of nearly synchronous bursts several hundred micrometres wide sweeps across neighbouring dots while distant dots remain quiet; then an inset of a live neonatal mouse visual pathway ('2012, live mice', schematic) echoes the same travelling wave to confirm it is not a dish artefact.

scenes.tts: Arrays also track cortical organoids, tissue grown in a dish, for months. In twenty nineteen, Trujillo, Muotri, and colleagues recorded these organoids on electrode arrays. They reported network oscillations growing more complex, with some features resembling brain-wave recordings, E E G, from preterm infants. Yet coordinated firing in tissue with no inputs is a long way from a working brain.
scenes.caption: Arrays also track cortical organoids, tissue grown in a dish, for months. In 2019, Trujillo, Muotri, and colleagues recorded these organoids on electrode arrays. They reported network oscillations growing more complex, with some features resembling brain-wave recordings, EEG, from preterm infants. Yet coordinated firing in tissue with no inputs is a long way from a working brain.
scenes.visual: The retina on the carried flat electrode array transforms into a rounded cortical organoid ('2019, months on array', schematic). On the right trace panel, scattered early spikes gradually organize into richer network oscillations (schematic); then a clear caution tag fades in beside the dish reading 'no inputs — not a working brain', gently crossing out the word 'mini-brain'.

scenes.tts: From retinal waves to organoid rhythms, arrays and probes reveal how whole populations act together. Still, big recording numbers demand care at every step. Count real neurons, analyse at the animal level, and match every claim to what was measured.

scenes.visual: The carried neural world settles into one calm view showing the probe shank and flat array on the left, live population traces in the middle, and three animal-level bars on the right (all schematic), each tier briefly lighting up in sequence as its check is named.
